propositions.text: The Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection and submits new evidence and requests an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: XXXXXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She alleges to be a citizen of Nigeria and no other country. The Appellant has submitted new evidence in support of her appeal and requests an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and substitute a positive determination or refer back for re-determination.
propositions.quote: She asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a positive determination or to refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection, submits new evidence, requests an oral hearing, and asks the RAD to set aside or refer back the decision.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and the matter is referred back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel under IRPA s.111(1)(c).
propositions.quote: This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal is allowed and the matter is referred back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel under IRPA s.111(1)(c).

propositions.text: The Appellant alleged to the RPD that she would be harmed by her father and others in Nigeria for refusing a forced marriage.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that, upon return to Nigeria, she will be harmed by her father and others because she refused to enter into a forced marriage.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleged to the RPD that she would be harmed by her father and others in Nigeria for refusing a forced marriage.

propositions.text: The RPD heard the claim on Nov 5, 2014 and rejected it on Nov 12, 2014.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on November 5, 2014. By a decision of November 12, 2014, the RPD rejected the claim.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant failed to establish identity on balance of probabilities and found her testimony about forced marriage not credible.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant failed to establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. It also found her testimony regarding being forced to marry a chief was lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD heard the claim in Nov 2014 and rejected it, finding the Appellant failed to prove identity and lacked credibility about forced marriage.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD erred in assessing evidence and rejecting identity documents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD committed errors in assessing her evidence and rejecting her identity documents.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the RPD erred in assessing evidence and rejecting identity documents.

propositions.text: What is the RAD's role in appeals against RPD decisions?
propositions.quote: What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD?

propositions.text: The Appellant refers to Huruglica, which found the RAD erred by applying reasonableness standard instead of independent assessment.
propositions.quote: The Appellant refers to Huruglica1 in her Memorandum. In Huruglica, the Court considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD. It found that the RAD had erred in simply reviewing the RPD's decision on a standard of reasonableness, rather than conducting its own independent assessment of the Appellants' refugee claims.

propositions.text: Huruglica held the RAD should not apply standard of review but consider purpose, statutory provisions, expertise, and appellate regimes.
propositions.quote: The Court held that the RAD's application of a reasonableness standard curtailed the tribunal's appellate role, contrary to the purpose of the RAD and the provisions of IRPA. In the Court's view, the RAD should not even engage in a standard of review analysis; rather, it should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the statutory provisions, comparable expertise, and comparative appellate regimes.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant cites Huruglica, which held the RAD erred by applying reasonableness standard instead of independent assessment, contrary to IRPA's purpose.

propositions.text: Huruglica requires the RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal, independently assessing refugee claims and substituting decisions if differing from RPD.
propositions.quote: Justice Phelan stated the following in Huruglica: 54. Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.

propositions.text: The RAD can respect RPD credibility findings but is not limited to intervening only for overriding errors.
propositions.quote: In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

paragraphs.summary: Huruglica requires the RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal with independent assessment, respecting but not limited by RPD credibility findings.

propositions.text: The RAD will independently assess the refugee claim, respecting RPD credibility findings but substituting its own decision if differing.
propositions.quote: The RAD will therefore review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, recognizing and respecting the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will independently assess the refugee claim, respecting RPD credibility findings but substituting its own decision if differing.

propositions.text: Under IRPA s.110(4), the Appellant may present only new evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available before.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of her claim or that was not reasonably available, or that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

propositions.text: The Appellant must make full submissions explaining how new evidence meets s.110(4) and relates to her claim.
propositions.quote: It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in her Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to her.

paragraphs.summary: Under IRPA s.110(4), the Appellant may present only new evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available before, with full submissions explaining relevance.

propositions.text: The Appellant tendered two new documents: a Nigerian passport photocopy issued in Ottawa and a letter authenticating her Nigerian driver's license.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has tendered two documents as proposed new evidence in support of her appeal. The first document is a photocopy of two pages from a Federal Republic of Nigeria passport issued in the Appellant's name in Ottawa on XXX 2014. The second document is a letter from the Nigeria High Commission in Ottawa, dated December 4, 2014, authenticating the Appellant's Nigerian driver's license.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant tendered two new documents: a Nigerian passport photocopy and a letter authenticating her Nigerian driver's license.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits she lacked money to obtain documents before RPD hearing and only got funds later from her church.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the proposed new evidence was not reasonably available to her at the time of her hearing before the RPD because she did not have the money to travel to the Nigerian embassy in Ottawa or to pay to obtain a new passport. She indicates that she was able to travel to Ottawa to obtain the documents only after her church provided her with the funds.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the new evidence is relevant to establishing her identity.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the proposed new evidence is relevant in resolving the issue of her identity.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits she lacked money to obtain documents before RPD hearing and that new evidence is relevant to her identity.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not explain why she lacked funds before rejection, but documents are dated after rejection and assist identity.
propositions.quote: The Appellant failed to indicate in her Memorandum why she was unable to obtain the funds to obtain her passport and authentication of her Nigerian driver's license prior to the rejection of the claim. Nonetheless, the documents are dated subsequent to the rejection of the claim by the RPD and would assist the Appellant in establishing her identity.

propositions.text: Since documents arose after rejection and are relevant to identity, they are accepted as new evidence on appeal.
propositions.quote: Since they arose after the rejection of the Appellant's claim and are highly relevant to the issue of her identity they will be accepted as new evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant did not explain lack of funds before rejection, but documents arose after rejection and are accepted as new evidence relevant to identity.

propositions.text: The Appellant requests an oral hearing under IRPA s.110(6) and RAD Rule 3(3)(d).
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks that an oral hearing be held, pursuant to Section 110(6) of IRPA and RAD Rule 3(3)(d).

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant requests an oral hearing under IRPA s.110(6) and RAD Rule 3(3)(d).

propositions.text: IRPA s.110(3) requires RAD to proceed without hearing on RPD record but allows accepting documentary evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: Section 110(3) of IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant.

propositions.text: Under s.110(4), the Appellant may present only new evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available before.
propositions.quote: The person who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA s.110(3) requires RAD to proceed without hearing on RPD record but allows new evidence under s.110(4).

propositions.text: Under s.110(6), RAD may hold hearing if new documentary evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision and justifies claim outcome.
propositions.quote: According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellant relies, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: In this appeal, with no Minister evidence, documentary evidence under s.110(3) must be understood in relation to s.110(4).
propositions.quote: In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: Under s.110(6), RAD may hold hearing if new evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision; here documentary evidence must be read with s.110(4).

propositions.text: Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) together mean RAD must not hold hearing unless new evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision and justifies claim outcome.
propositions.quote: When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) mean RAD must not hold hearing unless new evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision and justifies claim outcome.

propositions.text: New evidence assists in establishing identity but does not place Appellant in Nigeria at time of alleged incidents.
propositions.quote: It notes that the new evidence assists in establishing the Appellant's identity. However, neither of the documents entered as new evidence place the Appellant in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents that purportedly caused the Appellant to flee Nigeria in 2014.

propositions.text: The passport contains no info on departure from Nigeria; driver's license expired before alleged flight and does not place Appellant in Nigeria then.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's passport contains no information regarding her departure from Nigeria. The authentication of her Nigerian driver's license indicates that her driver's license expired on July 14, 2012, over two years before she allegedly fled Nigeria, and also does not place the Appellant in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents.

paragraphs.summary: New evidence helps establish identity but does not place Appellant in Nigeria at time of alleged incidents; passport and license lack relevant info.

propositions.text: New evidence does not justify allowing refugee claim; RAD must proceed without hearing and denies oral hearing request.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the new evidence does not justify allowing the Appellant's refugee protection claim. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing and the Appellant's request for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: New evidence does not justify allowing refugee claim; RAD proceeds without hearing and denies oral hearing request.

propositions.text: The RPD drew negative inference from Appellant not presenting Nigerian passport and not attempting to obtain new one after loss.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant not presenting a Nigerian passport as an identity document prior to her hearing. It noted that the Appellant made no attempt to obtain a new Nigerian passport after the passport she used to travel to the United States was taken by her agent.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD drew negative inference from Appellant not presenting Nigerian passport and not trying to get a new one after loss.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits she lacked money to obtain new passport before RPD hearing and only got funds later from church.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that, at the time of her hearing before the RPD, she did not have the money to travel to the Nigerian embassy in Ottawa or the money to pay to obtain a new passport. She indicates that she was able to travel to Ottawa to obtain the passport only after her church provided her with the funds.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD did not ask why she failed to obtain a new passport in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that she was not asked by the RPD why she had failed to obtain a new passport in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits she lacked money to get new passport before RPD hearing and was not asked why she failed to obtain it.

propositions.text: The RPD asked the Appellant why she had not tried to replace her Nigerian passport.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant was asked by the RPD at her hearing why she had not tried to replace her Nigerian passport.

propositions.text: The Appellant indicated she was not settled yet and so had not replaced her Nigerian passport.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated that she was not settled yet.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD asked the Appellant why she had not replaced her Nigerian passport; the Appellant said she was not settled yet.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted birth certificate, Nigerian driver's license and school certificate as identity evidence before and on hearing day.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submitted her certificate of birth,10 her Nigerian driver's license11 and a school certificate12 as identity evidence prior to and on the day of her hearing before the RPD.

propositions.text: The Appellant had been in Canada about three months before her hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant had been in Canada for approximately three months prior to her hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant's explanation for not replacing her Nigerian passport before the hearing was reasonable given her short time in Canada and identity documents presented.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's explanation for not having replaced her Nigerian passport prior to her hearing was reasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD does not agree with the RPD drawing a negative inference from the Appellant not presenting a Nigerian passport before her hearing.
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD does not concur with the RPD drawing a negative inference from the Appellant not presenting a Nigerian passport as an identity document prior to her hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted identity documents and had been in Canada three months; the RAD finds her explanation for no passport reasonable and rejects RPD's negative inference.

propositions.text: The RPD placed no weight on the Appellant's school certificate as identity evidence due to problems with the document.
propositions.quote: The RPD placed no weight on the Appellant's school certificate as evidence of her identity.

propositions.text: The RPD noted the photograph on the certificate was not discernable and could not confirm it was the Appellant.
propositions.quote: One problem noted was that the facial image in the photograph affixed to the certificate was not discernable and the RPD was unable to ascertain if the person in the photograph was the Appellant.

propositions.text: The word 'COPY' appeared throughout a section of the school certificate, raising concerns.
propositions.quote: It also noted that the word "COPY" appeared throughout a section of the certificate.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found problems with the school certificate's photo and 'COPY' markings and gave it no weight as identity evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD had insufficient reasons to reject her school certificate and erred by not giving her benefit of the doubt.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD had no sufficient reasons to reject her school certificate and committed errors by failing to give her the benefit of the doubt.

propositions.text: The Appellant notes the certificate was issued long ago in 2004.
propositions.quote: She notes that the certificate was issued a long time ago (2004).

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in rejecting her school certificate and notes it was issued long ago in 2004.

propositions.text: The Appellant's year of birth on school certificate differs from birth certificate.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant's year of birth on her school certificate13 differs from her year of birth on her birth certificate.14

propositions.text: The RPD did not address this discrepancy with the Appellant.
propositions.quote: However, the RPD did not address this discrepancy with the Appellant.

propositions.text: The RPD's issues with the school certificate are noteworthy but insufficient to discredit it without further analysis.
propositions.quote: The issues the RPD had with the school certificate, although noteworthy, are not sufficient to discredit the certificate entirely, without further analysis.

propositions.text: The RAD does not agree with the RPD that the school certificate holds no weight in establishing identity.
propositions.quote: As such the RAD does not concur with the RPD that the certificate holds no weight in establishing the Appellant's identity.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes birth year discrepancy on school certificate but finds RPD failed to analyze it and rejects RPD's dismissal of the certificate's weight.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a Nigerian driver's license unreasonable and illogical.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license in Nigeria unreasonable and illogical.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she got the license to establish identity for banking etc., not to drive, as she lacked passport and had expired NIC.
propositions.quote: It noted that the Appellant alleged she obtained her driver's license solely for the purpose of establishing her identity in Nigeria (for banking and other activities) and not to drive. The Appellant indicated to the RPD that, at the time she obtained her driver's license, she did not have her passport yet and her National Identity Card (NIC) had expired.

propositions.text: The Appellant said NIC expired annually, but documentary evidence showed NICs are issued for 10 years.
propositions.quote: She also indicated that the NIC expired annually. The RPD noted documentary evidence indicating that NICs are issued for 10 years.

propositions.text: The RPD found it unreasonable to take driving lessons just to get a license for identity when an identity card exists.
propositions.quote: It also noted that taking driving lessons, simply in order to obtain a driver's license for the purposes of establishing her identity for government and other related business in Nigeria, is unreasonable given there exists an identity card issued to all Nigerians for this stated purpose.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's explanation about her driver's license lacking credibility and noted prevalence of false documents in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellant's explanation regarding her driver's license lacking in credibility. The RPD also noted the prevalence of false documents in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a Nigerian driver's license unreasonable and lacking credibility, noting false documents are common in Nigeria.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues no evidence showed Nigerians cannot get driver's licenses solely for identity purposes.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that there was no evidence before the RPD that Nigerians cannot obtain a driver's license for the sole purpose of identity.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by assuming all Nigerian documents are fraudulent.
propositions.quote: It was also submitted that the RPD erred by assuming that all documents from Nigeria are fraudulent.

propositions.text: The Appellant notes none of her identity documents were issued in Benin City, where documents could be procured fraudulently.
propositions.quote: The Appellant noted that none of her identity documents were issued in Benin City where documentary evidence indicates that documents could be procured.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by assuming Nigerian documents are fraudulent and that no evidence showed driver's licenses can't be obtained solely for identity.

propositions.text: The Appellant's driver's license would be valid for 5 years, less than NIC's 10 years.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant's driver's licence would have been valid for less time than a NIC; five years compared to ten years.

propositions.text: The Appellant's claim that NICs expire annually contradicts documentary evidence and undermines her credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's assertion that NICs are valid for one year when the documentary evidence indicates that they are valid for ten years undermines her credibility.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect the Appellant to know NIC validity since she is educated and had one.
propositions.quote: It would be reasonable to expect her to know how many years a NIC is valid for since she is an educated woman who alleges she was in possession of a NIC.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges she considered renewing NIC before seeking driver's license as photo ID.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, she alleges she gave consideration to renewing her NIC before she sought another form of photo identification with a driver's license.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant's claim about NIC validity undermines her credibility and notes her driver's license is valid for less time than NIC.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to consider the driver's license document itself despite credibility concerns about reasons for obtaining it.
propositions.quote: While the RPD found that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license in Nigeria unreasonable, illogical and lacking in credibility, it failed to actually consider the document itself.

propositions.text: The driver's license has Appellant's name, photo, and security features like background printing and barcode.
propositions.quote: The national driver's licence15 has the Appellant's name and photograph and appears to have security features, including background printing and a bar code.

propositions.text: The RPD could have compared the license to a sample in evidence but apparently did not.
propositions.quote: The RPD could have compared this licence to a sample that was in evidence before it,16 but it does not seem to have done so.

propositions.text: It is unclear why the RPD found the driver's license did not assist the Appellant in establishing identity.
propositions.quote: It is unclear from the RPD's reasons why this document does not assist the Appellant in establishing her identity.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD failed to consider the driver's license document itself and unclear why it was dismissed as identity evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees the Appellant's reasons for obtaining driver's license lack credibility.
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD concurs with the RPD that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license lacks credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant's lack of knowledge about NIC validity undermines her credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant's lack of knowledge about the validity period of a NIC, when it would be reasonable to expect her to know this undermines her credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD disagrees with the RPD dismissing the driver's license as an identity document altogether.
propositions.quote: However, the RAD does not concur with the RPD in dismissing the Appellant's Nigerian driver's license, as an identity document, altogether.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees the Appellant's reasons for the driver's license lack credibility but rejects dismissing the license as identity evidence entirely.

propositions.text: The RPD noted the birth certificate was issued in 1996 though Appellant was born in 1989.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Appellant's birth certificate was issued in 1996, when she was born in 1989.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she did not know why the birth certificate was issued in 1996 and did not know whereabouts of original.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated to the RPD that she did not know why it was issued in 1996 and did not know the whereabouts of her original birth certificate.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's explanations for the birth certificate date were not reasonably explained.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellant's explanations for the date on her birth certificate were not reasonably explained.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's explanations for the birth certificate date discrepancy unreasonable and unexplained.

propositions.text: The RAD disagrees with RPD's finding on birth certificate as RPD failed to explain why Appellant's explanations were unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD does not concur with the RPD's finding regarding the birth certificate. The RPD indicates that the Appellant's explanations were not reasonable but fails to indicate why they were not reasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD must explain reasons for credibility findings to be respected on review.
propositions.quote: The RPD is required to explain the reasons for their findings. Without reasons, it is difficult for the RAD to recognize and respect this credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD failed to explain why the Appellant's birth certificate explanations were unreasonable, undermining respect for that finding.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges her boyfriend was attacked by her father, chief, and four thugs in January 2014 after she visited him.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that in January 2014, after visiting her boyfriend, her father, the chief she was to marry and four thugs attacked her boyfriend.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified the boyfriend was punched and dragged for 30 minutes; she witnessed the attack.
propositions.quote: She testified at her hearing before the RPD that her boyfriend was punched and dragged for approximately 30 minutes by the four thugs and she witnessed the attack.

propositions.text: The Appellant said boyfriend did not need medical attention or bleed but had bruises on jaw.
propositions.quote: She also indicated that her boyfriend did not need medical attention, nor was he bleeding, but had bruises on his jaw.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's account of the beating lacking credibility as it was unreasonable that four men beat a man for 30 minutes without medical need or bleeding.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellant's account of the beating lacking in credibility. It noted that it was unreasonable and incredible that four men could beat and drag another man for 30 minutes and the victim not require medical attention or the beating did not result in any bleeding.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified her boyfriend was beaten for 30 minutes with bruises but no bleeding; the RPD found this account not credible.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues she did not contradict her claim about boyfriend's injuries and that 30 minutes was approximate time.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that she did not contradict her claim when she testified that her boyfriend was not injured but sustained only bruises after he was beaten by four thugs for about 30 minutes.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by assuming all beatings cause hospitalization and impugning her credibility perversely.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD committed an error in perversely impugning her credibility and evidence by assuming that every beating that involved slapping and kicking would always result in hospitalization.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in assuming all beatings cause hospitalization and wrongly impugned her credibility about boyfriend's injuries.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with RPD that the Appellant's account of boyfriend's beating lacked credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with the RPD's finding that the Appellant's account of the beating of her boyfriend lacked credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified boyfriend was beaten, punched, kicked and dragged for 30 minutes by four men.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified before the RPD that her boyfriend was beaten, punched, kicked and dragged on the street by four men for approximately 30 minutes.

propositions.text: It is absurd to suggest boyfriend suffered only bruises after such a brutal attack.
propositions.quote: It is absurd for the Appellant to suggest that her boyfriend suffered no injuries except bruising after being brutally attacked by four men for approximately 30 minutes.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect medical treatment and bleeding from such an attack.
propositions.quote: It would be reasonable to expect the victim of such an attack to require medical treatment for injuries sustained in the attack. It would also be reasonable to expect the victim of such an attack to suffer lacerations and experience bleeding.

propositions.text: The Appellant's assertion that boyfriend only had bruising further undermines her credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's assertion that her boyfriend only had bruising on his face and jaw, when such an attack would likely cause more serious injuries, further undermines the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant's account of boyfriend's beating lacking credibility as it is unreasonable he had only bruises after a brutal 30-minute attack.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges she was held against her will for two days after boyfriend's beating and sneaked out on third day to visit him.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that, following the incident when her boyfriend was beaten, she was forced to return home and held against her will for two days. She testified before the RPD that she managed to sneak out of her home on the third day to see her boyfriend and returned home afterwards.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she returned home because she did not believe her father was serious about the marriage.
propositions.quote: When asked by the RPD why she returned home after visiting her boyfriend, the Appellant indicated that she did not believe her father was serious about the marriage.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she believed father was not serious because no wedding date was set despite witnessing beating and being held captive.
propositions.quote: When asked why she believed her father was not serious about the marriage, considering that she had witnessed the beating of her boyfriend with the chief present and was held against her will, the Appellant indicated that it was because a wedding date had not been set.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's explanation for returning home unreasonable and lacking credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellant's explanation for returning to her family home, after all that had transpired, unreasonable and lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges she was held captive, sneaked out to visit boyfriend, but returned home believing father was not serious; RPD found this explanation not credible.

propositions.text: The RPD considered the Gender Guidelines in assessing the Appellant's actions.
propositions.quote: In assessing the Appellant's actions, the RPD noted that it considered the Gender Guidelines.

propositions.text: The Appellant refused to marry the Chief and witnessed violence against her and boyfriend.
propositions.quote: It noted that the Appellant had indicated her refusal to marry the Chief and had witnessed violence directed towards her and her boyfriend.

propositions.text: The RPD found it unreasonable that the Appellant would return home after sneaking out, given the violence and no wedding date set.
propositions.quote: It found that it was unreasonable, when the Appellant had an opportunity to sneak out of the home and did so, that she would return home simply because a marriage date had not been set.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's account lacking credibility as she chose to return to family home after escaping captivity.
propositions.quote: It further found the Appellant's account of the event lacking in credibility as she had an opportunity to leave and chose to return to the family home where she had just escaped being held captive.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the Appellant's allegation of threat to marry the chief lacked credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the Appellant's allegation of the threat of having to marry a chief was lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's explanation for returning home after escaping captivity unreasonable and lacking credibility, concluding her forced marriage claim lacked credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD failed to properly apply the Gender Guidelines to her claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to properly apply the Gender Guidelines to her claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD wrongly concluded the Guidelines require immediate flight at first opportunity.
propositions.quote: She argues that the RPD wrongly concluded that the Gender Guidelines require a young woman, such as her, fleeing forced marriage to immediately flee at the first opportunity.

propositions.text: The Appellant says her boyfriend encouraged her to flee and she was unemployed and dependent on parents, making fleeing difficult.
propositions.quote: She argues that it was her boyfriend who finally encouraged her to flee her home and go to Lagos to hide with her aunt. She argues that the RPD failed to consider the evidence that she was unemployed, was dependant on her parents for support and the difficulty she would face if she had decided to flee to a new location where she would have nobody to depend on for support.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD misapplied Gender Guidelines and failed to consider her dependency and boyfriend's role in fleeing.

propositions.text: The RPD referenced Gender Guidelines but provided no analysis related to them.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that, while the RPD made reference to the Gender Guidelines, it provided no analysis in relation to the Gender Guidelines.

propositions.text: Gender Guidelines require considering women's ability to travel safely and stay without hardship when assessing internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The Gender Guidelines indicate that, in determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative (IFA), decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship.

propositions.text: Decision-makers should consider religious, economic, cultural factors affecting women in IFA reasonableness.
propositions.quote: It is further noted in the Gender Guidelines that in determining the reasonableness of an IFA, the decision-makers should take into account factors including religious, economic, and cultural factors, and consider whether and how these factors affect women in the IFA.

propositions.text: The RPD's analysis of Appellant's return home should have assessed her action under Gender Guidelines regarding IFA reasonableness.
propositions.quote: Although IFA was not a determinative issue in the RPD decision, its analysis of the Appellant's action of returning home after escaping would justify assessing her action under this area of the Gender Guidelines as it questions the Appellant's reasons for not fleeing the family home to an alternate location at a particular time.

propositions.text: The RPD's findings on Appellant's return home are not supported by Gender Guidelines and failed to address her circumstances and reasonableness of fleeing.
propositions.quote: The RPD's findings in this area are not supported by the Gender Guidelines. It failed to address the Appellant's circumstances and the reasonableness of fleeing when she initially escaped her home.

propositions.text: The RAD does not agree with RPD that Appellant's explanation for returning home was unreasonable and lacking credibility.
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD does not concur with the RPD finding that the Appellant's explanation for returning to her family home was unreasonable and lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD failed to analyze the Gender Guidelines properly and rejects RPD's finding that Appellant's return home was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD raised failure to claim asylum in the US but did not address it in its decision.
propositions.quote: The RPD raised failure to claim elsewhere as an issue at the Appellant's hearing however failed to address the issue in its decision.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she traveled to the US on a visa because it was faster to get than a Canadian visa.
propositions.quote: At her hearing the Appellant indicated that she travelled to the United States on a visa because it took less time to obtain a visa for the United States than Canada.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she did not claim asylum in the US because she knew Canada was her final destination.
propositions.quote: When asked by the RPD why she did not make an asylum claim in the United States, the Appellant said that she knew that Canada was her final destination.

propositions.text: The Appellant said she stayed in the US about six weeks while agent arranged a fraudulent Canadian passport.
propositions.quote: She also indicated that she remained in the United States for approximately six weeks while her agent made arrangements to obtain a fraudulent Canadian passport for her.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified her agent took her genuine Nigerian passport upon arrival in the US and requested $2,000 more for Canadian passport.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified at her hearing before the RPD that her agent took her genuine Nigerian passport from her as soon as she arrived in the United States. She also indicated that the agent requested an additional $2,000 from her to secure a Canadian passport for her but she did not have the money.

propositions.text: The Appellant said the agent held her Nigerian passport as payment.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated that the agent held her Nigerian passport as payment.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD raised failure to claim asylum in US but did not address it; the Appellant said she traveled to US on visa, stayed six weeks, and agent took her passport for fraudulent Canadian passport.

propositions.text: The Appellant traveled to the US in 2014, stayed until August 13, then entered Canada without filing asylum in the US.
propositions.quote: The Appellant traveled to the United States on XX, 2014 and remained there until August 13, 2014, when she entered Canada. She did not file an asylum claim in the United States.

propositions.text: At RPD hearing, Appellant said her final destination was Canada and her agent in Nigeria told her Canada was best for abused women.
propositions.quote: At her hearing before the RPD, when asked why she did not claim asylum in the United States, the Appellant indicated that her final destination was Canada. When asked how she first found out about Canada and when she decided to come to Canada, the Appellant indicated that her agent in Nigeria told her Canada was the best place for abused women.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant traveled to the US in 2014, did not claim asylum there, and said her agent told her Canada was best for abused women.

propositions.text: Appellant traveled to US with genuine Nigerian passport and valid visa but entered Canada with fraudulent passport without claiming refugee protection at border.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant travelled to the United States using a genuine Nigerian passport. She had a valid visa for the United States... The Appellant entered Canada using a fraudulent passport and did not claim refugee protection in Canada at the Canadian border.

propositions.text: Appellant's explanation for not claiming asylum in US is unreasonable given she was safe there with genuine documents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's explanation for not claiming asylum in the United States is unreasonable. She arrived in the United States, a safe country, with genuine documents and a valid visa.

propositions.text: It is unreasonable Appellant left safe US with genuine documents to enter Canada with false documents risking deportation to Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it unreasonable that the Appellant left the United States where she was safe and had entered with genuine documents and entered Canada with false documents and ran the risk of being deported to Nigeria where she alleges she faced persecution or harm.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant used genuine documents to enter US but fraudulent ones to enter Canada, making her explanation for not claiming asylum in US unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD takes judicial notice that the US is a democratic country with excellent human rights record, especially for abused women.
propositions.quote: The RAD takes judicial note of the fact that the United States is a highly democratic country with an excellent human rights record, especially with respect to abused women.

propositions.text: An educated person fearing persecution is expected to seek refugee protection in the first safe country they reach.
propositions.quote: It would be reasonable to expect an educated person such as the Appellant to have pursued refugee protection in the United States if she feared returning to Nigeria as alleged. One would expect a person fearing persecution or harm in their home country to pursue refugee protection in a safe country they have travelled to. The Federal Court has indicated that a person fleeing persecution is expected to seek protection in the first safe place.

propositions.text: RAD draws negative inference on Appellant's allegations of persecution risk in Nigeria due to failure to claim asylum in US without reasonable explanation.
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD draws a negative inference with respect to the Appellant's allegations that she faces a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm in Nigeria. The RAD further finds that the Appellant's failure to claim in the United States, without a reasonable explanation, undermines her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes US is safe and expects refugees to claim asylum there first; Appellant's failure undermines her credibility and allegations of risk in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Appellant provided affidavits from aunt and pastor to RPD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant provided the RPD with an affidavit from her aunt, as well as an affidavit from her pastor.

propositions.text: RPD presumed to consider all evidence but must analyze and explain disregarding evidence contrary to its decision.
propositions.quote: The RPD is presumed to have considered all of the evidence before it, and there is no requirement for the RPD to refer to each document in the record. However, where there is evidence which is contrary to its decision, the RPD must analyze that evidence and provide reasons why it does not consider it relevant or trustworthy, or why it chose to disregard it.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant gave affidavits to RPD; RPD must analyze and explain disregarding contrary evidence.

propositions.text: RPD made no reference to affidavits corroborating Appellant's story and consistent with her Basis of Claim.
propositions.quote: In this case, the RPD simply made no reference to the affidavits, which corroborate parts of the Appellant's story and is consistent with her Basis of Claim (BoC) narrative.

propositions.text: RPD concluded Appellant's evidence was not credible regarding threats of forced marriage to a chief.
propositions.quote: Instead, the RPD concluded that the Appellant's evidence was not credible in respect to threats of having to marry a chief.

paragraphs.summary: RPD ignored affidavits supporting Appellant's story and found her evidence not credible on forced marriage threats.

propositions.text: RPD may have dismissed affidavits due to disbelief of boyfriend's beating or Appellant's return home after escape.
propositions.quote: It may be that the RPD dismissed the affidavits because it did not believe that the Appellant's boyfriend was beaten or that the Appellant would return home after initially escaping.

propositions.text: RPD's finding on Appellant returning home after escape is problematic, making rejection of affidavits equally problematic.
propositions.quote: However, as noted above, the RPD's finding, with respect to the Appellant returning home after having initially escaped, is problematic. As such, that rejection of the affidavits is equally problematic.

paragraphs.summary: RPD's disbelief of boyfriend's beating and return home is problematic, so its rejection of affidavits is also problematic.

propositions.text: Appellant asks RAD to set aside RPD decision and substitute a positive determination.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a positive determination.

propositions.text: RAD cannot substitute positive determination due to multiple identity and credibility concerns and lack of questioning Appellant.
propositions.quote: The RAD is in no position to do so. There were multiple identity and credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence and the RAD is unable to make that determination only on the basis of the RPD record and new evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant's year of birth differs on school and birth certificates; identity documents do not place her in Nigeria at alleged incident times.
propositions.quote: For example, the Appellant's year of birth on her school certificate differs from her year of birth on her birth certificate. Furthermore, none of Appellant's identity documents place her in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents.

propositions.text: Biometric data sharing could help establish Appellant's identity and countries of reference.
propositions.quote: Biometric information through the Five Country Conference High Value Data Sharing Protocol would assist in establishing the Appellant's countries of reference, an aspect of her identity...

propositions.text: RAD has not seen or questioned Appellant and cannot reach conclusions on identity or credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD has not seen or questioned the Appellant and therefore cannot reach its own conclusions on all relevant aspects of her identity or credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant asks RAD to substitute positive decision; RAD declines due to identity and credibility issues and lack of questioning.

propositions.text: Appellant asks RAD to refer matter back to RPD for re-determination.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Appellant asks that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

propositions.text: RAD agrees to refer matter back to RPD for re-determination.
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with this remedy.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant requests referral back to RPD; RAD agrees to this remedy.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed; RPD determination set aside; matter referred to RPD for re-determination by different panel under IRPA s.111(1)(c).
propositions.quote: This appeal is allowed and the determination of the RPD is set aside. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal allowed; RPD decision set aside; matter referred to RPD for re-determination by different panel.
